{{short description|American physicist and electrical engineer}}
[[File:Barbara_Kegerreis_Lunde.jpg|thumb|Barbara Kegerreis Lunde at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in 1964.]]
'''Barbara Kegerreis Lunde''' (born 1937) is an American [[physicist]] and [[Electrical engineering|electrical engineer]]. She worked for [[NASA]] in the 1960s, where she developed several instruments for various projects. Lunde became the second woman to graduate from [[Iowa State University]] with a doctorate in physics and the first woman in [[Iowa]] to become a professional electrical engineer.

== Biography ==
Lunde, the daughter of an [[electrical engineer, physicist and radiologist]], grew up in [[Elmhurst, Illinois]].<ref name=":3" /> She graduated from [[York Community High School]] in 1955.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://thisisyork.org/11096/features/under-the-monocle-dr-barbra-kegerris-lunde/|title=Under the Monocle: Dr. Barbara Kegerreis Lunde|last=Fanelli|first=Matt|date=8 November 2016|website=This is York|access-date=2019-06-29}}</ref> After high school, she earned a bachelor's and master's degree in physics at [[Northwestern University (United States)|Northwestern University]] in 1957 and 1959, respectively.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|date=Spring 2015|title=Alumni Focus|url=https://www.physics.northwestern.edu/documents/dimensions/dimensions-springsummer2015.pdf|journal=Dimensions|pages=7}}</ref> After graduation, Lunde was hired at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]], working on the design of [[guidance system]]s for the [[LGM-30 Minuteman|minuteman missile]].<ref name=":0" /> Also while at MIT, she developed and later patented a digital [[accelerometer]].<ref name=":1" /> In 1961, she started working as an engineer at the [[Goddard Space Flight Center]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://dp.la/browse-by-topic/women-in-science/space-exploration|title=Space Exploration|website=Digital Public Library of America|access-date=2019-06-29}}</ref> where helped develop a more simple jet propellant system for use in space.<ref name=":3" /> She also worked as project manager on the Reliable Earth Sensor.<ref name=":1" /> Early in her career, Lunde recalls that she was often the only woman at scientific conferences.<ref name=":3">{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/33433935/|title=Lady Scientist's Credo for the Job: 'Feminine But Not Distracting'|date=30 June 1964|work=Daily Republican-Register|access-date=1 July 2019|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>

Lunde moved to [[Ames, Iowa]] where she helped build a radio station and where she also started studying at [[Iowa State University]].<ref name=":1" /> The radio station, [[KOEZ (FM)|KLFM]], co-owned with her husband Paul, was built and maintained by Lunde.<ref name=":4">{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/33434402/|title=KLFM: Built, Run by a Lady|last=Bryson|first=Michael|date=4 September 1970|work=Des Moines Tribune|access-date=1 July 2019|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> Later in 1970, she became the second woman to  graduate from Iowa State with a doctorate in physics.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=http://www.elmhurst205.org/16DoD|title=2016 Dukes of Distinction|date=2016|website=Elmhurst Community School District 205|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170427201915/http://www.elmhurst205.org/16DoD|archive-date=27 April 2017|access-date=29 June 2019|url-status=live}}</ref> Lunde was also the first woman to become a professional [[Electrical engineering|electrical engineer]] in [[Iowa]].<ref name=":2" /> Lunde also worked as an assistant professor at Iowa State.<ref name=":4" /> In the 1980s, another job emerged from her work in radio, when Lunde started creating [[Undergarment|underwear]] to protect wearers from [[electromagnetic radiation]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/33369576/the_des_moines_register/|title=Engineer Mining for a Market for Silver-Lined Underwear|last=Collins|first=Lisa|date=7 March 1988|work=The Des Moines Register|access-date=1 July 2019|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> She called the company Silver Lining.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/33315026/the_indianapolis_star/|title=Look for a Silver Lining|date=21 December 1986|work=The Indianapolis Star|access-date=1 July 2019|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>

Lunde started working as an aerospace technologist for the FAA in 2003 as a Training Specialist.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite journal|date=February 2012|title=15th Annual FAA Commercial Space Transportation Conference Speakers|url=https://www.faa.gov/about/office_org/headquarters_offices/ast/media/Conference_Speakers.pdf|journal=Federal Aviation Administration|pages=16}}</ref> She retired in 2013 and moved to [[Minneapolis]].<ref name=":1" /> In 2015, she was honored with a Richard S. Alberg Distinguished Science and Technology Professional Award.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://mfests.org/awards/distinguished-scientists-and-technologists/|title=Distinguished Scientists and Technologists|date=2015-06-15|website=Minnesota Federation of Engineering, Science, and Technology Societies|access-date=2019-06-29}}</ref>
